title: Experiment: change one thing, check fairly, decide by a rule written first
outcomes: Designs a two-way comparison of training methods that changes one thing and keeps the rest fixed
Writes a prediction and a decision rule before any data
Chooses a fair check: new positions, no idea named, some look-alikes where the practised idea fails
Reads two small scores with their ranges and says whether they can be told apart

steps.text: An **experiment** changes one thing and keeps the rest the same, so a difference can be blamed on the change. *Example:* practise forks **blocked** (all forks in a row) for two weeks, then forks **interleaved** (mixed with other themes) for two weeks, same minutes, with a check on new mixed positions after each. Two good sessions prove nothing. You need a measure, a check on positions you did not practise, and a decision rule written *before* you look.

In a block of forks you know the idea before you look; a **fair check** does not tell you. Rules of thumb: (1) positions you did not practise, not a mirror of one; (2) no idea named; (3) some positions where the practised idea fails, or 'always fork' scores full marks; (4) the same check for both methods. Compare two methods on one skill, not forks against pins; the order can also fool you (by the second fortnight you know more). Four silent positions follow as a tiny check.

steps.title: The same fork, one change
steps.prompt: A check made only of the first kind of position cannot tell skill from habit. Predict, then check.

steps.text: **How much does a score show?** The My plan page prints a rough range for each score. With 8 items: 2 right is 7%-59%, 4 right 22%-78%, 6 right 41%-93%, 8 right 68%-100%. A start of 3 of 8 and a check of 6 of 8 sounds like a doubling, yet the ranges overlap. 'Cannot tell' means not enough data, not 'no effect'. A plan that shows nothing, or goes down, is still data.

steps.prompt: Press Save note to see the answers. Ranges for 8 items: 1 right 2%-47%, 2 right 7%-59%, 7 right 53%-98%, 8 right 68%-100%. With 4 items, 3 right is 30%-95%. Your four silent answers form a tiny check.

fields.label: How many of the four silent positions did you get right on the first try, with no hints?
Baseline (your starting score) 2 of 8. What is the smallest check score out of 8 whose range lies completely above the baseline range (above 59%)?
Baseline 1 of 8, check 8 of 8: can the two ranges be told apart?

steps.text: **What the app does for you now, and when it stops.** My plan keeps one skill, your goal, a 'what would tell you it worked' box and the check date. It runs a silent baseline, then a silent check on up to 8 positions from families you did not meet at baseline, and shows the ranges. It cannot compare two methods, and two plans would draw different positions: keep a paper log. Write your rule in the success box before the baseline. Do not delete a failed plan.

steps.prompt: Design your own experiment. Write the prediction and the decision rule now, before any data. A plan that fails is a result, not a mistake.

fields.label: The one thing that differs between method A and method B:
What I keep the same (minutes, days, check format):
My check: new positions, no idea named, some where the idea fails:
I will keep the change if ... and drop it if ...:
If the ranges overlap I will:
The biggest thing that could fool me:
